# Phenylketonuria (PKU)

Sharon F. Daley; Andres Morales.

#### Authors

Sharon F. Daley 1; Andres Morales 2.

#### Affiliations

 1 Cape Cod Hospital, Hyannis, MA

 2 Columbia University

Last Update: April 12, 2026.

## Continuing Education Activity

Phenylketonuria, also known as phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency, is an inborn error of metabolism most commonly caused by pathogenic or pathogenic variants in the gene encoding phenylalanine hydroxylase—the hepatic enzyme that converts phenylalanine to tyrosine. Phenylketonuria is classified as an aminoacidopathy, or toxic accumulation disorder, in which excess substrate, specifically phenylalanine and its metabolites, produces neurotoxicity if untreated. Biochemically, phenylketonuria is characterized by elevated blood phenylalanine concentrations and a relative tyrosine deficiency. Affected newborns typically appear normal at birth; however, without treatment, progressive manifestations develop over the first months of life and may include a musty or mousy odor of the skin or urine, hypopigmentation, eczema, irritability, tremors, seizures, and neurocognitive impairment.

 Objectives: 

- Identify the genetic and biochemical basis of phenylketonuria and recognize its clinical presentation across the lifespan.
- Apply current American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics guideline recommendations for diagnosis, monitoring, and treatment of patients with phenylketonuria.
- Evaluate traditional and emerging therapies, including dietary management, pharmacologic options, and investigational gene and messenger RNA–based approaches.
- Implement effective interprofessional strategies to coordinate care, communicate management plans, and support long-term adherence for individuals with phenylketonuria.

## Introduction

Phenylketonuria (PKU), also known as phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) deficiency, is one of the earliest recognized inborn errors of metabolism and remains a paradigm for diagnosing and treating genetic metabolic diseases. First described by the Norwegian biochemist and physician Asbjørn Følling in the 1930s, based on observations of abnormal phenylalanine metabolites in affected children, PKU later became the foundation for modern newborn screening programs, with the development of a simple bacterial inhibition assay in the 1960s. [1] PKU is the most common disorder caused by an inborn error of amino acid metabolism. [2] Early detection and dietary intervention have transformed PKU from a cause of severe intellectual disability into a largely treatable condition, underscoring the critical importance of timely recognition and lifelong metabolic management.

PKU is most commonly caused by mutations in the gene encoding PAH, a primarily hepatic enzyme that catalyzes the hydroxylation of phenylalanine to tyrosine (see Image. PKU and Role of PAH, BH4, Melanin, and Phenyl Ketones). [2] The disorder is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner, and pathogenic variants reduce or eliminate PAH activity in affected individuals. Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) serves as an essential cofactor by binding to the catalytic domain of PAH and enabling this metabolic conversion. PKU is classified as an aminoacidopathy, or toxic accumulation disorder, in which excess substrate—phenylalanine and its metabolites—produce neurotoxicity if untreated. Biochemically, PKU is characterized by elevated blood phenylalanine concentrations and a relative tyrosine deficiency.

Affected newborns typically appear normal at birth; however, without treatment, progressive manifestations emerge over the first months of life and may include a musty odor of the skin or urine, irritability, tremors, seizures, microcephaly, and neurocognitive impairment. These neurological and developmental features reflect the developing brain's vulnerability to sustained hyperphenylalaninemia (HPA). Tyrosine is a precursor of the skin pigment melanin, and reduced tyrosine causes hypopigmentation of the skin and hair. The musty odor in individuals with PKU is caused by phenylacetic acid, a metabolite of phenylalanine that accumulates and is excreted in sweat, urine, and skin secretions.

This activity reviews the etiology, epidemiology, pathophysiology, clinical presentation, evaluation, and management of PKU, emphasizing early detection through newborn screening and lifelong metabolic control. This activity incorporates the 2025 American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics guideline–based recommendations, highlights recent therapeutic advances, and discusses emerging investigational approaches, such as gene and messenger RNA therapies, aimed at restoring PAH activity. This activity emphasizes the role of coordinated, interprofessional care in optimizing outcomes across the lifespan.

## Etiology

PKU is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the PAH gene, which encodes the enzyme PAH. This autosomal recessive disorder results in deficient PAH activity and impaired conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine, leading to the biochemical phenotype of elevated blood phenylalanine levels and relative tyrosine deficiency. Carriers with a single functional allele typically maintain sufficient enzymatic activity to prevent disease. [3] The PAH gene is located on chromosome 12q23.2, and hundreds of likely pathogenic or pathogenic variants have been identified worldwide, most of which reduce PAH activity through protein misfolding, instability, or decreased expression. [4] [5] As a result, phenylalanine cannot be adequately metabolized, leading to its accumulation and reduced tyrosine production. Under normal conditions, phenylalanine, an essential amino acid, is tightly regulated to support protein synthesis while remaining at nontoxic concentrations.

The most common pathogenic variant replaces arginine with tryptophan at codon 408 (p.Arg408Trp) and is strongly associated with classic PKU, a traditional PAH terminology, in which blood phenylalanine levels typically exceed 1200 µmol/L. Some variants retain residual enzyme activity and are associated with less severe phenotypes, including mild PKU (blood phenylalanine levels of 600 to 1200 µmol/L) and mild HPA (blood phenylalanine levels below 600 µmol/L). Approximately 73% of individuals with PKU are compound heterozygotes, carrying 2 distinct PAH variants rather than identical or homozygous variants. [6] About 27% are homozygous for a single pathogenic PAH variant. [4] Genotype combinations influence metabolic severity, such as severe-severe or severe-mild allele pairings, contributing to the clinical spectrum of disease. [7]

Overall, PKU is a disorder of impaired enzymatic function with significant allelic heterogeneity, and the specific genetic variants largely determine residual PAH activity, biochemical phenotype, and therapeutic responsiveness.

## Epidemiology

PKU has a global prevalence estimated at approximately 1 in 10,000 to 24,000 live births, with rates varying widely by ethnicity and geographic region, ranging from 1 in 4500 in Italy to 1 in 125,000 in Japan. An estimated 450,000 individuals worldwide are affected. [3] [4] [8]

- Europe: Overall prevalence is roughly 1 in 10,000 live births, with notable regional variation. Turkey reports the highest rates (1 in 2600 to 1 in 4000), which are believed to be at least partly attributable to higher consanguinity. Northern Ireland and Italy each report a prevalence of 1 in 4500, whereas Finland has among the lowest prevalence (1 in 100,000 to 1 in 200,000). A geographic gradient exists, with classic PKU more common in Eastern Europe and milder phenotypes (mild PKU and HPA) predominating in southwestern and southern Europe. [4] [8] [9]
- United States: Incidence is approximately 1 in 15,000 live births, with state-specific rates ranging from 1 in 13,500 to 1 in 19,000. [6] [8] [9] [10] PKU is more frequent among Whites and Native Americans and less common among Black, Hispanic, and Asian populations. Over 10,000 individuals are estimated to have PKU in the United States. [10] [11]
- Asia: Prevalence varies widely from 1 in 15,000 to 1 in 100,500. China reports 1 in 15,000 to 100,500; Japan, 1 in 70,000 to 125,000; and Thailand, less than 1 in 200,000. [4] [9]
- Latin America: Reported prevalence ranges from 1 in 25,000 to 1 in 50,000, with higher rates in southern regions.
- Africa: PKU appears rare, though precise data are limited. [9]

 Phenotype Distribution 

Globally, approximately 62% of cases are classic PKU, 22% are mild PKU, and 16% are mild HPA. The proportion of classic PKU increases from Europe (56%) to the Middle East (71%) to Australia (80%), reflecting population-specific patterns of PAH variants. [4]

 Carrier Frequency 

Carrier frequency depends on ethnicity and is estimated at approximately 1 in 50 among individuals of Northern European descent. [10]

## Pathophysiology

PKU results from a deficiency of PAH, the rate-limiting hepatic enzyme that converts phenylalanine to tyrosine and requires BH4, molecular oxygen, and iron as cofactors. Loss of PAH activity due to biallelic pathogenic variants impairs phenylalanine metabolism, leading to the accumulation of phenylalanine and its toxic metabolites—phenylpyruvate, phenylacetate, and phenylactate—in the blood and brain, along with a relative tyrosine deficiency. The disorder is characterized by both substrate toxicity and a deficiency of downstream products, including catecholamine neurotransmitters, melanin, and other tyrosine-derived compounds. [3] [9]

Elevated phenylalanine readily crosses the blood-brain barrier and disrupts cerebral amino acid transport by competitively inhibiting the uptake of other large neutral amino acids, such as tyrosine and tryptophan. This inhibition reduces brain concentrations of these precursors and impairs the synthesis of key neurotransmitters, including dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine, and serotonin, contributing to abnormalities in neurodevelopment and function. [8] Tyrosine deficiency also reduces melanin production, explaining the hypopigmentation often observed in untreated individuals. [3]

The neurologic manifestations of PKU arise from multiple interconnected mechanisms and are not solely due to phenylalanine toxicity. Proposed contributors include altered neurotransmitter metabolism, decreased cerebral protein synthesis, impaired bioenergetics, oxidative stress, and white matter abnormalities. The severity of clinical disease correlates with the degree of residual PAH activity, determined by the specific genotype, producing a spectrum from classic PKU to mild HPA. [8]

Some less severe variants encode enzymes with altered affinity for the PAH cofactor BH4 or demonstrate increased stability in the presence of BH4. This molecular variability helps explain why an estimated 49% of patients respond to pharmacologic BH4 supplementation, typically defined as a reduction of at least 30% in blood phenylalanine levels despite normal endogenous BH4 concentrations. [6] [9]

Overall, the pathophysiology of PKU reflects a loss-of-function metabolic block that disrupts phenylalanine homeostasis, leading to toxic metabolite accumulation and a deficiency of critical neurochemical substrates during vulnerable periods of brain development.

## History and Physical

Infants with PKU appear normal at birth, and diagnosis is typically made through routine screening before symptoms develop. Universal newborn screening has largely prevented the classic untreated phenotype in many countries. Without early identification and treatment, clinical signs and symptoms emerge gradually over the first months to years of life.
